position.summary: The text describes Iraq navigating three overlapping pressures simultaneously in late September 2026. A drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, launched from Iraqi territory on September 11, gave Riyadh a strong argument that Baghdad did not fully control its armed factions. The U.S. military withdrawal from Iraq entered its final visible phase, with end-of-September deadlines approaching for the last troops in northern Kurdish areas. Iraq's Prime Minister Zaidi prepared to visit the United States, attend UN General Assembly events, and meet President Trump. Baghdad formally requested a six million barrel-per-day OPEC quota amid Hormuz disruption and elevated global oil prices. A pilot road-transport operation was moving southern crude to Kirkuk for export via Turkey. ADNOC had purchased discounted Iraqi crude and talks with TotalEnergies had opened. Iraq had lifted decade-old restrictions on western civilian airspace and set a phased reopening schedule for Iran border crossings. The KRG and Baghdad were coordinating on northern export logistics as U.S. bases emptied.

naive_forecast.summary: The naive reading takes Scenario A at face value, treating the 55-to-60 percent base case as the week's script. Baghdad publicly blames a named militia splinter for the Saudi pipeline attack, completing its domestic narrative of controlled discipline. The Iraqi PM meets Trump at the UN, signaling stability and asking for post-exit security reassurance. U.S. forces finish their northern withdrawal with a coordinated KRG handover statement. Iraq expands its road-transport of southern crude to Kirkuk for Turkey-bound exports. OPEC+ formally approves Iraq's six million barrel-per-day quota request. The week plays out as a sequence of visible, checkable wins: the exit completes, the blame lands on a named group, the oil flows north, and Europe signs on. Each problem gets a clean resolution that lets Baghdad claim sovereign competence over the entire period.

crystal_forecast.summary: The crystal reading prices the full 55-to-60 percent base case against the 20-to-25 percent diplomatic de-escalation scenario and the 15-to-20 percent militia escalation tail risk. The PM's Trump meeting and the phased Iran border reopening still anchor the week, but the crystal forecast explicitly assigns real probability to a PMF faction striking a Saudi or Gulf energy target before October 8, forcing Baghdad into a public-discipline-versus-private-tolerance squeeze. It also acknowledges that a regional Hormuz or pipeline arrangement from Oman, Riyadh, or Tehran would shift Iraq's OPEC leverage and European energy negotiations in Baghdad's favor. The text's own hedges, that formal OPEC approval in seven days is unlikely, that the PMF weapons-stay statement is ritual, and that the militia-blame narrative stops short of naming top leaders, pull probabilities down on the cleanest outcomes and up on the partial, messier ones.
crystal_forecast.reasoning: The naive reading treats the 55-to-60 percent Scenario A as the script and ignores the text's explicit allocation of 20-to-25 percent to diplomatic de-escalation and 15-to-20 percent to militia escalation. The crystal reading substitutes the OPEC formal-quota event with a Scenario-B regional Hormuz arrangement, because the text says a full OPEC+ decision in seven days is unlikely. It raises the militia-attack probability to 0.18, drawing on the text's description of the PMF weapons-stay statement as almost a ritual and its labeling of Scenario C as the dangerous one. It keeps the border reopening and PM-visit events near their text-stated confidence because the text hedges them less. The core difference: the crystal reading treats the combined 40 percent non-base-case probability as a set of real, checkable outcomes rather than background noise.
